questions.q: Define natural vegetation and state the three primary environmental controls that determine its type in India.
questions.a: Natural vegetation is plant cover that grows without human aid and remains undisturbed long enough to reach climatic climax. The three controls are: (1) precipitation (amount and seasonality), (2) temperature (mean annual and range), and (3) relief/soil (altitude, aspect, drainage). A wrong answer that omits "undisturbed by humans" or lists only rainfall reveals confusion between natural vegetation and planted forests/crops, or a failure to integrate temperature and relief as independent controls.

questions.q: Why do Tropical Evergreen forests occur on the windward side of the Western Ghats but not on the leeward side, even though both receive rainfall from the same monsoon system?
questions.a: The windward side receives orographic rainfall >200 cm annually with no distinct dry season, meeting the evergreen threshold of >200 cm and short dry period. The leeward side lies in a rain shadow, receiving <100 cm with a pronounced dry season, favoring deciduous or thorn types. A student who answers "both get rain so both should be evergreen" misunderstands the critical role of rainfall seasonality and the rain-shadow effect, confusing total annual rain with effective moisture availability.

questions.q: Given a station at 12°N latitude, 800 m altitude, with annual rainfall 150 cm and a dry season of 4 months, identify the natural vegetation type and justify using climatic thresholds.
questions.a: Step 1: Note rainfall 150 cm → falls in 100-200 cm range (deciduous zone). Step 2: Dry season 4 months → distinct dry period, not evergreen. Step 3: Altitude 800 m at 12°N → mean annual temperature ~22°C (using lapse rate 6.5°C/km from sea-level ~27°C), well within tropical range. Step 4: Combine → Tropical Moist Deciduous Forest. A wrong answer of "Evergreen" ignores the dry season length; "Thorn" misreads the rainfall threshold.

questions.q: Compare the climatic envelopes of Tropical Dry Deciduous and Tropical Thorn forests. Explain why the latter replaces the former along a rainfall gradient from east to west in the Deccan Plateau.
questions.a: Tropical Dry Deciduous: 75-100 cm rainfall, dry season 5-6 months. Tropical Thorn: <75 cm rainfall, dry season >6 months. Moving westward across the Deccan, rainfall declines from ~100 cm to <50 cm due to increasing distance from Bay of Bengal branch and rain shadow of Western Ghats. The longer, more intense drought selects for xerophytic adaptations (thorns, succulence, deep roots), causing a gradual floristic shift. A student who attributes the change solely to temperature or soil misses the primary driver: decreasing moisture availability and increasing aridity index.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Montane forests in the Himalayas are simply cooler versions of tropical forests found at lower altitudes." Provide two specific reasons why this is incorrect.
questions.a: The statement is incorrect. Reason 1: Montane forests show distinct altitudinal zonation (subtropical pine → temperate broadleaf → coniferous → alpine) driven by temperature lapse rate, not a uniform cooling. Reason 2: Species composition changes fundamentally (e.g., sal replaced by oak, then deodar, then fir) with new genera/families appearing, not just stunted tropical species. A student who agrees confuses temperature as the only variable, ignoring that photoperiod, frost, snow cover, and soil development also shift with altitude, creating discrete biome boundaries.

questions.q: Design a climatic criteria table (columns: Forest Type, Annual Rainfall Range, Dry Season Length, Mean Annual Temperature Range) for the five major natural vegetation types of India. Use it to predict the vegetation type for a hypothetical location at 28°N, 2000 m altitude, 180 cm rainfall, 3-month dry season.
questions.a: A good table lists: Tropical Evergreen (>200 cm, <1 month dry, >22°C), Tropical Moist Deciduous (100-200 cm, 3-4 months, >22°C), Tropical Dry Deciduous (75-100 cm, 5-6 months, >22°C), Tropical Thorn (<75 cm, >6 months, >22°C), Montane (variable rain, temperature-driven zones). For the given location: altitude 2000 m at 28°N → MAT ~10°C (lapse rate), rainfall 180 cm, dry season 3 months → falls in Montane Wet Temperate zone (150-250 cm, 10-15°C). A poor answer forces it into Tropical Moist Deciduous ignoring the temperature drop with altitude, showing failure to apply altitudinal zonation.
